exercises.title: Action vs Event: Lightning Round
exercises.prompt: Drop each statement into the right zone: purposeful action or mere event.

items.text: Alice flips a coin to decide whether to quit her job.
A rock rolls down a hill.
Bob buys a coffee to stay awake during a study session.
A volcano erupts and showers ash on a town.
Carla absentmindedly taps her foot to music.
Derek slams the door to signal he’s angry.
Eve ducks under a flying frisbee before it hits her.
Lena sprints for the bus after checking the schedule.

exercises.title: Means–Ends Match
exercises.prompt: Crusoe’s goals: stay warm, fish more tomorrow, impress Friday. Last turn he chose B: gather firewood. Which read is praxeologically sound?
options: He revealed B ≻ A and B ≻ C at that moment; it’s ordinal, not about his feelings’ intensity.
He proved he cares more about impressing Friday than survival, because firewood is social signaling.
You can now rank his happiness in utils: firewood = 10, net = 8, nap = 1.
The choice is random noise; without a survey we learn nothing.

exercises.title: Opportunity Cost Snap
exercises.prompt: You have one hour before a flight: study econ notes, call a friend, or scroll social media. You called a friend. What’s the opportunity cost?
options: The next-best forgone option—whatever you ranked just below calling—probably studying.
All other options you didn’t pick, lumped together.
Only the money you didn’t earn while chatting.
There is no cost because chatting is relaxing.

exercises.title: Crusoe to Market: Find the Trade Line
exercises.description:
Three castaways: A, B, C. Stocks: A has fish, B has coconuts, C has stone tools.
Wants now: A wants coconuts, B wants tools, C wants fish.
exercises.prompt: Which move actually gets A coconuts fastest and shows the onset of indirect exchange?

choices.label: A trades fish directly to B for coconuts; double coincidence holds.
choices.feedback: Correct. Direct exchange works because B wants fish and A wants coconuts—no detours needed.

choices.label: A trades fish to C for tools, then C trades tools to B for coconuts; A waits for leftovers.
choices.feedback: Too many steps: A could already trade directly. Indirect exchange matters when direct coincidence fails.

choices.label: A waits for "proto-money" rules; no one trades until a decree arrives.
choices.feedback: Exchange emerges from wants, not permission slips. Waiting creates no coconuts.

exercises.title: Calculation Check: Socialist Manager
exercises.description:
You run a planning bureau. Physical data: tons of steel, labor hours, and machines. No market for capital goods—only "social value points" assigned by a board.
Projects:
- X: Monumental bridge.
- Y: Expand housing blocks.
exercises.prompt: Can you pick the economically best use of capital?

choices.label: Yes. Compare social points per ton of steel and choose the higher ratio.
choices.feedback: Ratios of arbitrary points are not market prices. They don’t reveal opportunity costs of capital goods.

choices.label: No. Without money prices for factors, any choice is a guess; technical data alone is not economic calculation.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Calculation needs market prices for capital goods to compare alternatives. Otherwise you’re steering blind.

choices.label: Partly. Use last year’s prices forever; they never go stale.
choices.feedback: Shadow prices without live markets drift. Praxeology’s point: real prices arise from current exchange, not frozen tables.

exercises.title: Intervention Cascade: Price Ceiling
exercises.prompt: A binding price ceiling is imposed below the market-clearing price. Sort each consequence.

items.text: Chronic shortage at the controlled price.
Non-price rationing like queues or favoritism.
A surplus piling up unsold at the controlled price.
Quality deterioration or shrinkflation to cope with the cap.
The ceiling instantly raises the market-clearing quantity.
